messages.subject: Optimization and Variable Model Components
parts:
I've created the code (below) to fit a series of time-varying peaks to a surface, the parameters of which each evolve using random walks. It works very well, however, it runs extremely slowly (5-8 hours on an Nx=50  x Ny=100 matrix).

Is there anything obvious that I can do to speed this up? The exponents in my model are time-varying I can't precompute them, and I can't vectorize the ^ operation. I ultimately want to be able to have more than 3 peaks, and right now the model fit time is impractical for use.

Assuming this can run in a reasonable time, I would also like to be able to determine the optimal number of peaks at each time, such that
       surface(t)=sum(In * Pn(params)) where n=1:number of peaks
meaning that the surface at time t is the sum of several peaks (P1...PN), each of which has an indicator function (Ip) dictating whether they are on or off.

Even better would be letting the indicator functions switch on/off based on some estimated markov probability. I know stan doesn't estimate discrete parameters like this, and I had a few thoughts of how to approach this problem. One way might be to create some transition probability parameter for each component and perform a test against a pseudorandom number at each time to determine if a switch occurs. Alternatively, I could try all possible combinations indicator functions at a given time and choose based on maximum likelihood, which I believe is similar to marginalizing out the discrete parameter.

Any thoughts?

Thanks!!


data {
    int<lower=0>         Nx; //number of xvals
    int<lower=0>         Ny; //number of yvals

    vector[Ny]           y_vals; //y values
    matrix[Nx, Ny]       surface; //surface
}

parameters{
    //Peak 1
    real<lower=8, upper=35>     peak1_Ft[Nx];
    real<lower=0, upper=20>     peak1_At[Nx];
    real<lower=5, upper=100>    peak1_Bt[Nx];

    real<lower=.8, upper=5>     peak1_sig2Ft;
    real<lower=0>               peak1_sig2At;
    real<lower=0>               peak1_sig2Bt;

    //Peak 2
    real<lower=0, upper=1>      peak2_Ft[Nx];
    real<lower=0>               peak2_At[Nx];
    real<lower=0, upper=2>      peak2_Bt[Nx];

    real<lower=0, upper= 1>     peak2_sig2Ft;
    real<lower=0>               peak2_sig2At;
    real<lower=0>               peak2_sig2Bt;

    //Peak 3
    real<lower=1, upper=3>      peak3_Ft[Nx];
    real<lower=0>               peak3_At[Nx];
    real<lower=1, upper=10>     peak3_Bt[Nx];

    real<lower=0, upper= 1>     peak3_sig2Ft;
    real<lower=0>               peak3_sig2At;
    real<lower=0>               peak3_sig2Bt;

    //Baseline
    real<lower=0>               baseline_At[Nx];
    real<lower=0, upper=1>      baseline_Rt[Nx];
    real                        baseline_Ot[Nx];

    real<lower=0>               baseline_sig2At;
    real<lower=0>               baseline_sig2Rt;
    real<lower=0>               baseline_sig2Ot;

    //Observation Noise
    real<lower=0, upper=10>      sig2obs;
}


model {
    //Model variables
    matrix[Nx, Ny] mu; //Holds the mean

    //Gamma parameters
    real peak1_k;
    real peak1_theta;
    real peak2_k;
    real peak2_theta;
    real peak3_k;
    real peak3_theta;
   
    //Priors
    peak1_Ft[1] ~ normal(20,5);
    peak2_Ft[1] ~ normal(.1,.5);
    peak2_Bt[1] ~ normal(.1,.05);
    peak3_Ft[1] ~ normal(1,2);
    peak3_Bt[1] ~ normal(2,.5);

    baseline_Ot[1] ~ normal(-25,5);
    baseline_Rt[1] ~ normal(.01,.001);
    baseline_At[1] ~ normal(50,10);

    sig2obs ~ cauchy(0,.5);    
 
    for (x in 1:Nx){
       if(x>1)
        {
            //Create Random Walk
            peak1_Ft[x] ~ normal(peak1_Ft[x-1], peak1_sig2Ft);
            peak1_At[x] ~ normal(peak1_At[x-1], peak1_sig2At);
            peak1_Bt[x] ~ normal(peak1_Bt[x-1], peak1_sig2Bt);

            peak2_Ft[x] ~ normal(peak2_Ft[x-1], peak2_sig2Ft);
            peak2_At[x] ~ normal(peak2_At[x-1], peak2_sig2At);
            peak2_Bt[x] ~ normal(peak2_Bt[x-1], peak2_sig2Bt);

            peak3_Ft[x] ~ normal(peak3_Ft[x-1], peak3_sig2Ft);
            peak3_At[x] ~ normal(peak3_At[x-1], peak3_sig2At);
            peak3_Bt[x] ~ normal(peak3_Bt[x-1], peak3_sig2Bt);

            baseline_At[x] ~ normal(baseline_At[x-1], baseline_sig2At);
            baseline_Rt[x] ~ normal(baseline_Rt[x-1], baseline_sig2Rt);
            baseline_Ot[x] ~ normal(baseline_Ot[x-1], baseline_sig2Ot);
        }

        //Compute Gamma Terms
        peak2_k=(sqrt(peak2_Ft[x]^2*(4*peak2_Bt[x]+peak2_Ft[x]^2))+2*peak2_Bt[x]+peak2_Ft[x]^2)/(2*peak2_Bt[x]);
        peak2_theta=(sqrt(peak2_Ft[x]^2*(4*peak2_Bt[x]+peak2_Ft[x]^2))-peak2_Ft[x]^2)/(2*peak2_Ft[x]);

        peak3_k=(sqrt(peak3_Ft[x]^2*(4*peak3_Bt[x]+peak3_Ft[x]^2))+2*peak3_Bt[x]+peak3_Ft[x]^2)/(2*peak3_Bt[x]);
        peak3_theta=(sqrt(peak3_Ft[x]^2*(4*peak3_Bt[x]+peak3_Ft[x]^2))-peak3_Ft[x]^2)/(2*peak3_Ft[x]);

        peak1_k=(sqrt(peak1_Ft[x]^2*(4*peak1_Bt[x]+peak1_Ft[x]^2))+2*peak1_Bt[x]+peak1_Ft[x]^2)/(2*peak1_Bt[x]);
        peak1_theta=(sqrt(peak1_Ft[x]^2*(4*peak1_Bt[x]+peak1_Ft[x]^2))-peak1_Ft[x]^2)/(2*peak1_Ft[x]);

        for (y in 1:Ny){
            //Add baseline
            mu[x,y] = baseline_At[x]*(1-baseline_Rt[x])^y_vals[y]+baseline_Ot[x];
   
            //Add Peak 1
            mu[x,y] = mu[x,y] + peak1_At[x]/(exp(1-peak1_k)*((peak1_k-1)*peak1_theta)^(peak1_k-1))*y_vals[y]^(peak1_k-1)*exp(-y_vals[y]/peak1_theta);

            //Add Peak 2
            mu[x,y] = mu[x,y] + peak2_At[x]/(exp(1-peak2_k)*((peak2_k-1)*peak2_theta)^(peak2_k-1))*y_vals[y]^(peak2_k-1)*exp(-y_vals[y]/peak2_theta);
   
            //Add Peak 3
            mu[x,y] = mu[x,y] + peak3_At[x]/(exp(1-peak3_k)*((peak3_k-1)*peak3_theta)^(peak3_k-1))*y_vals[y]^(peak3_k-1)*exp(-y_vals[y]/peak3_theta);
        }
    }
 
      to_vector(surface) ~ normal(to_vector(mu), sig2obs);
}

> {

> peak1_Ft[x] ~ normal(peak1_Ft[x-1], peak1_sig2Ft);

And in that second one, there's clearly a lot of repeated
computation of 1 - peak1_k (and its negation). Save these and reuse.
> The exponents in my model are time-varying I can't precompute them, and I can't vectorize the ^ operation.
Vectorizing ^ wouldn't add any speed --- loops are fast in Stan.

> I ultimately want to be able to have more than 3 peaks, and right now the model fit time is impractical for use.
>

> meaning that the surface at time t is the sum of several peaks (P1...PN), each of which has an indicator function (Ip) dictating whether they are on or off.

You can also fit models with different numbers of peaks and
compare. Stan's not really set up to do this kind of nonparametrics
(with varying numbers of parameters across MCMC iterations). You
could think about it as a Dirichlet process or something, but at
best you'd be able to approximate that in Stan.

> Even better would be letting the indicator functions switch on/off based on some estimated markov probability. I know stan doesn't estimate discrete parameters like this, and I had a few thoughts of how to approach this problem. One way might be to create some transition probability parameter for each component and perform a test against a pseudorandom number at each time to determine if a switch occurs.

That won't work with Stan's samplers as it introduces
a huge discontinuity that'll block the Hamiltonian Evolution.

> Alternatively, I could try all possible combinations indicator functions at a given time and choose based on maximum likelihood, which I believe is similar to marginalizing out the discrete parameter.

You can't do that choosing within the model for the same reason
as the previous comment.

You can actually just marginalize it out if the combinatorics isn't too bad
(it's 2^N in number of variables).

- Bob

foo[t] ~ normal(g(foo[t-1]), sigma);

as

You have to use the for loop. It's because of this:
bg_At[2:Nx] = bg_At[1:(Nx-1)] + bg_At_raw[2:Nx]*bg_sig2At;

C++ is pass by value, but the values can be references (don't
blame me, I just wrestle with C++).

In the C++ translation of a Stan function call, primitives are
passed by pure value, as in (double x) or (int x), whereas any structures
(arrays or matrices) are passed by const reference, as in
(const Eigen::Matrix<T, L, R>& x).

If you do

X = foo(X)

then X is only set after foo(X) is evaluated.

- Bob
